title: The assistant who reads for you

beats.say: What if you could send an assistant to read twenty files, and they came back with just a ten line note?

That is a subagent. Picture a busy manager at her desk. Instead of reading every report herself, she sends an assistant to the archive. The assistant has their own desk, their own instructions and their own set of tools.
The assistant reads everything, then returns only a short summary. The manager's desk stays tidy, so she can think clearly about her next decision.
The catch is that the assistant's time costs money, and the trip takes a while. For a one line question, just ask it yourself.

check.q: In the analogy, why does the manager send an assistant instead of reading the reports herself?
opts: So her own desk stays uncluttered and she can focus on decisions
So the reports are read faster than anyone could read them
So that the assistant can make the final decision for her
check.why: A subagent does the heavy reading in its own space and returns a short summary, which keeps the main conversation small and focused.

work: Name one task you do that involves reading many files just to answer a small question.
Next time you must search a large codebase, ask yourself whether a helper could return only a summary.

title: Where the twenty file reads go

beats.say: Where do twenty file reads go when a subagent does the work? Not into your main conversation.

The main session sends a task. The subagent starts fresh, with its own context window, its own instructions and its own tool list. It reads twenty files, maybe forty thousand tokens, searching and running tests.
When done, it returns only a summary, about ten lines, maybe three hundred tokens. Your main context grows by three hundred, not forty thousand.
That matters because every later turn re-reads the whole conversation. Smaller context means cheaper turns and a more focused main agent.

check.q: A subagent reads forty thousand tokens of files and returns a three hundred token summary. What grows in the main context?
opts: About forty thousand tokens
About three hundred tokens
Nothing, since summaries are free
check.why: Only the returned summary enters the main conversation. The file reads stay in the subagent's own context window.

work: Delegate your next broad codebase search to a subagent and compare how much your main conversation grew.
Ask for a summary of roughly ten lines so the return stays small.

title: Why the subagent missed it

beats.say: Why did your subagent miss something you discussed ten minutes ago?

show.text: It missed what you said earlier.

beats.say: Because it has its own context window. It does not see your conversation. Whatever it needs, the file names, the goal, the constraints, must be written into the task you hand over.

The return trip is lossy too. Only the summary comes back. If the subagent finds twelve things but reports three, the main agent never sees nine. Ask for exactly what you need, such as file paths and line numbers.
Its tools are its own list as well. A reviewer given read-only tools cannot edit files, which is the point. Give the minimum it needs.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Put full context in the task
Ask for paths and line numbers

check.q: A subagent gives a wrong answer because it ignored a constraint you set earlier in the chat. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The constraint was never included in the task you handed over
The subagent ran out of file handles
Subagents ignore all constraints by design
check.why: A subagent has its own context window and does not see the main conversation, so everything it needs must be in its task and instructions.

work: Write a task template with goal, files, constraints and the exact format you want back.
Request file paths and line numbers in every summary so you can verify claims.
Give review subagents read-only tools.

title: When a subagent is not worth it

beats.say: When is a subagent a waste of money?

show.text: When is a subagent a waste?

beats.say: Every subagent burns its own tokens and adds latency. For a one-line question, like what does this function return, asking directly is cheaper and faster.
It pays off when work is broad, like searching a large codebase, or independent, like a review, where reading a lot produces a little. Use it when input is big and the answer is small.
Use it for focus too. A reviewer with a checklist and read-only tools beats a generalist halfway through implementing. Decide by the ratio of tokens read to tokens returned.

check.q: Which task is the weakest candidate for a subagent?
opts: Searching a large repo for every use of a deprecated API
Reviewing a diff with a checklist and read-only tools
Asking what a single known function returns
check.why: A one-line question costs more in subagent tokens and latency than it saves. Subagents pay off when much is read and little is returned.

work: Set a rule of thumb: delegate when you expect to read many files but need only a short answer.
Give review work to a subagent with a checklist and read-only tools.
Track subagent token spend so the cost stays visible.

title: A subagent is a specialist with a job card

beats.say: What if you could hire a specialist, hand over one short job card, and know they cannot touch anything you did not allow?

show.text: A specialist with a job card
show.sub: and a short list of allowed tools

beats.say: A subagent is that specialist. It is a helper that Claude can call in for one kind of task. Its job card is a small text file with a name, a description of when to use it, and a list of allowed tools.
Think of a building inspector. They may look at everything, but they carry no hammer. They write a report and leave. So a reviewer gets tools to read, not tools to edit.
Claude reads the description like a job title, and calls the right helper by itself. Or you can simply ask for it by name.

show.title: Two ways to call it
items: Claude matches the task to the description
Or you ask for the helper by name

check.q: In the inspector analogy, why does a reviewer helper get only read tools?
opts: Read tools run faster
A reviewer only needs to look and report, so it should not be able to change anything
Edit tools cost extra money
check.why: Give a helper only what its job needs. A reviewer reports findings, so edit access is needless risk.

work: Pick one repeated chore, like code review, that could be handed to a helper.
Write its job in one sentence, then list the fewest tools it needs.

title: How a subagent file works

beats.say: How does a markdown file become a teammate that Claude can call?

Put the file in dot claude slash agents inside the project, and your whole team shares it. Put it in your home folder under dot claude slash agents, and it stays personal. Or run slash agents to build one interactively.
The top has four fields: name, description, tools, and model. Below that is plain text, the system prompt, which tells the helper who it is and what to report.

show.title: pipeline-reviewer.md
show.text:
name: pipeline-reviewer
description: Reviews pipeline changes. Use after any change under pipeline/.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
---
You are a senior data engineer reviewing a change. Do not edit files.

beats.say: Our reviewer runs git diff, runs the unit tests, and returns at most eight ranked findings, ending with approve or request changes. Claude matches your task to the description, then hands off.

check.q: Which field mostly decides when Claude calls the helper on its own?
opts: model
description
tools
check.why: Claude matches the current task against each helper's description. Tools limit what it can do, and model picks the brain.

work: Create one helper in .claude/agents/ and commit it so teammates get it.
Specify the output format in the prompt, such as a cap on findings and a final verdict.

title: Where subagent definitions go wrong

beats.say: Why did your subagent never get called, or worse, edit a file it should not?
Automatic delegation depends on the description. A vague one like helps with code never matches. Say what it checks and when: use after any change under pipeline. Good descriptions are the trigger.

Leave out the tools line and the helper inherits everything, including edit. Even a reviewer with Bash can still write files through shell commands, so also say in the prompt: do not edit files. Tools are the fence; the prompt is the sign.

show.title: Tools are the fence, prompt is the sign
items: No tools line means it inherits everything
Bash can still write files via shell
So also write: do not edit files

beats.say: Also, a subagent starts with a fresh context. It does not see your chat, so the prompt must say how to get the diff and what output to return. Demand a concrete failing input, or findings turn into vague opinions.

check.q: A helper has Bash but no Edit tool and its prompt is silent on editing. What is the risk?
opts: None, since Edit is missing
It could still change files through shell commands
It will refuse to run git diff
check.why: Bash can write files with shell commands, so omitting Edit is not a full guarantee. State the rule in the prompt and keep Bash only if needed.

work: Rewrite any vague description to say what it checks and when to use it.
Always set an explicit tools line instead of inheriting everything.
Put the diff command and output format inside the helper's prompt.

title: When a subagent is the right call

beats.say: When is a subagent the wrong tool?

show.text: When is it the wrong tool?

beats.say: Use one when the work is read heavy and noisy, like reviewing a diff. The helper burns its own context reading files, and returns only a short report. Your main conversation stays clean.

Skip it for small tasks. Each helper pays startup cost, rereads files, and spends tokens. A one-line fix does not need a team. Pick a cheaper model like sonnet for review volume, and keep the strongest model for hard design calls.

show.title: Skip it when
items: The task is tiny, like a one-line fix
Use a cheaper model for volume work

beats.say: Share project agents in git so reviews are consistent, but treat them like code: review changes to them. For hard guarantees, do not trust a model reviewer. Use an automated build gate. Subagent review is advice, not enforcement.

chip.text: Hard rules belong in the gate

check.q: Which task is the best fit for a subagent?
opts: Fixing a typo in one line
Reviewing a large diff that needs reading many files and running tests
Enforcing a must-never-break data rule
check.why: Subagents shine on read-heavy, noisy work that returns a short report. Tiny fixes waste tokens, and hard rules need an automated gate.

work: Keep project subagents in git and review changes to them like code.
Back any rule that must never break with an automated check, not only a reviewer helper.
Match model to task: cheaper for routine review, stronger for design decisions.

title: Two cooks, one cutting board

beats.say: What happens when two cooks try to use one tiny cutting board at the same time?
Chaos. Ingredients mix, and nobody knows whose chopping is whose. Two AI helpers in one project folder do the same thing. They overwrite each other's files.

show.sub: Two helpers, one place to work

beats.say: A git worktree gives each helper its own station: a separate folder on its own branch, which is just a named line of changes. Both stations share one pantry, the single repository holding all the history.
When both finish, a person checks each dish, then the changes are combined back in the main folder.

check.q: Why does a worktree stop two AI helpers from overwriting each other?
opts: Each gets its own folder and branch, sharing one repository
It makes the helpers take turns
It copies the project to the cloud
check.why: Each helper edits files in a separate folder on a separate branch, so their edits cannot collide until a reviewed merge, while the history stays in one shared repository.

work: Name one task you do in a project folder that could be done by two helpers at once.
Try making a worktree on a practice repo and see the new folder appear.

title: Setting up two worktrees

beats.say: How do you run two Claude sessions on one repository without them stepping on each other?

First, run git worktree add with a new folder and a new branch name. Do it twice: one for amounts, one for loader. Each folder is a full working copy on its own branch, fix slash amounts and fix slash loader.

show.title: Create two worktrees
show.text:
git worktree add ../cc-amounts -b fix/amounts
git worktree add ../cc-loader -b fix/loader

beats.say: Second, open a terminal in each folder and start Claude. Session one edits only the amounts folder. Session two never sees those edits, so nothing collides.
Third, back in the main folder, review each branch, then merge both. Finally, git worktree remove deletes the extra folders.

check.q: After both sessions finish, what is the right order?
opts: Remove the worktrees, then review
Review each branch, merge, then remove the worktrees
Merge without review, then review later
check.why: A person reviews each branch first, then merges into the main folder, and only then removes the extra worktrees.

work: Create two worktrees for two unrelated fixes and start a session in each.
Write down which files each task touches before you start.

title: Where parallel worktrees break

beats.say: Why does parallel work still go wrong, even with separate folders?

show.sub: Files are split. Logic is not.

beats.say: Worktrees isolate files on disk, not logic. If both branches edit the same file, the folders are fine but the merge conflicts. And if task two needs task one's result, it builds on a guess.

Git also refuses to check out one branch in two worktrees, to stop double edits. And each folder is a fresh checkout, so ignored files like env settings or installed packages are missing until you set them up.
Remove finished worktrees, or stale folders pile up.

show.title: Clean up
show.text:
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../cc-amounts
git worktree prune

check.q: Two worktree tasks both need to change the same helper file. What is the best move?
opts: Run them in parallel and fix the conflict later
Run them one after the other
Check out the same branch in both worktrees
check.why: Overlapping files turn into merge conflicts. Tasks that touch the same files should run sequentially. Git also blocks one branch in two worktrees.

work: Before parallelising, list the files each task will touch and check for overlap.
Add a setup step for env files and dependencies to your worktree routine.

title: When parallel worktrees pay off

beats.say: If agents are cheap, why not run ten in parallel?

Because the bottleneck moves to you. Each branch still needs one human reviewer, so ten branches means ten reviews. Token cost also grows with every session, while the speed gain stops where your review time runs out.
Worktrees are cheap on disk because they share one repository, unlike full clones. But they share one machine, so ports and databases can still clash. Use containers when you need stronger isolation.
If tasks touch the same files or depend on each other, go sequential. Use subagents for read-only research inside one session. Pick two or three truly independent tasks.

check.q: What mainly limits the benefit of running many worktree sessions at once?
opts: Git allows only two worktrees
Human review of each branch and rising cost
Branches cannot be merged
check.why: Git permits many worktrees, but each branch needs a reviewer and each session costs tokens, so gains flatten once review time is saturated.

work: Cap parallel sessions at what you can review the same day.
Decide up front which tasks need containers, subagents, or sequential runs instead.

title: One cook or a whole kitchen?

beats.say: Would you hire a whole kitchen crew to make one sandwich?

show.sub: Picking how many agents to use

beats.say: Of course not. One cook can do most jobs. That is a single agent: one loop of thinking, acting, and checking. It is simple and cheap.
Bigger jobs need helpers. Scouts search many shelves at once and report back. An editor reads the writer's work with fresh eyes. A head chef hands forty orders to line cooks.

show.title: Helpers for bigger jobs
items: Scouts search many shelves at once
Editor reviews the writer with fresh eyes
Head chef splits forty orders among cooks

beats.say: But every extra cook costs wages, and cooks can bump into each other. So hire a crew only when the work truly splits into separate pieces.

chip.text: Hire only for truly separate work

check.q: When is hiring several agents instead of one most justified?
opts: Whenever the task feels important
When the work splits into truly separate pieces
When you want the answer to look more thorough
check.why: Extra agents add cost and coordination, so they pay off only when the work is genuinely parallel or needs separate expertise.

work: Default to one agent for your next task and note where it struggles.
List tasks you have that split into independent pieces.

title: Four agent patterns, step by step

beats.say: Your agent must migrate forty dbt models. Do you run one agent or forty?
A single agent is one loop. Its weakness is context growth: on long tasks the history fills up and early details get lost. Subagents help by giving a side job a fresh, empty context.
In explore, the main agent fans out searches. Each subagent reads many files, then returns only a short summary. The main context stays small.
In orchestrator and workers, a planner splits the forty models into independent pieces. Workers run in parallel, and the planner merges the results.
In writer and reviewer, a fresh agent checks the change against a checklist.

check.q: Why does a subagent help the main agent on a big codebase search?
opts: It reads files faster than the main agent
It works in a fresh context and returns only a summary
It removes the need for any summary
check.why: The subagent's file reading stays in its own context, so the main agent keeps a small context and receives only a short result.

work: Pick one long task and try a subagent for the search part only.
Write down which of your jobs are independent enough for workers.

title: Where multi-agent setups break

beats.say: Why can a subagent's summary make your agent confidently wrong?
A summary is lossy. A subagent might read fifty files and report five lines. A detail like a nullable column or an odd join key can vanish, and the main agent never knows it was there.
Parallel workers have another trap. Two workers edit the same shared macro, and the merge conflicts. Give each worker its own files, or its own branch.
Reviewers fail quietly too. Told only to review this, a fresh agent often approves. Hand it a real checklist: row counts match, tests pass, no schema drift.

show.title: A real review checklist
items: Row counts match the old model

beats.say: Finally, coordination itself costs tokens. Planner and workers all re-read shared instructions.

check.q: Two parallel workers keep producing merge conflicts. What is the best fix?
opts: Add a third worker to resolve them
Give each worker separate files or its own branch
Ask the reviewer to approve faster
check.why: Conflicts come from overlapping edits, so partition the work so workers never touch the same files.

work: Ask subagents to return key facts, such as columns and keys, not just a summary.
Write a concrete review checklist before using a reviewer agent.
Assign each parallel worker its own files or branch.

title: When a crew is the wrong choice

beats.say: When is a team of agents worse than one agent?
Often. Multi-agent runs can use several times the tokens of a single agent. If one agent costs one dollar, a fan-out of ten workers might cost five or more, plus planner overhead.
So use them only when work is genuinely parallel, like forty independent models, or needs separate expertise, like writing then reviewing.
Otherwise, start with one agent. Trim its context, add a checklist, and write better tests first.
Then measure. Compare quality, speed, and cost against the single agent baseline. If the crew does not win on those numbers, drop it.

check.q: A team proposes an orchestrator with ten workers for a sequential, tightly coupled task. What should you do?
opts: Approve it, since more agents means better quality
Start with a single agent and measure before adding more
Add a reviewer and skip measuring
check.why: Sequential, coupled work gains little from parallelism while cost and coordination rise. A measured single agent baseline shows whether more agents help.

work: Record tokens, time, and quality for a single agent baseline.
Require a measured gain before approving any multi-agent design.
